_about: Every slide in the course, described in plain words. choose_register.py sends 'brief' to Jev. 'shapes' are my own reading of the content against the content-shape rules; Jev never sees them, they are only used to check Jev's pick.

slides.title: TypeSafe Jev: The Complete Hands-On Course
slides.brief: The front page of a full engineering course about one AI model. The course name, the instructor and the edition, with a drawing of what the model does: a question goes into the model, a probability comes out, and plain code then acts, checks again, or hands the case to a person.

slides.title: 300 tickets in 12.6 seconds, for less than one cent
slides.brief: The opening moment of the course: 300 customer support tickets were each sorted by team, urgency and mood in 12.6 seconds, and the whole job cost 0.74 of one US cent. Measured numbers from a real run, shown so the size of the result is clear at once.

slides.title: Who this course is for
slides.brief: Eight groups of engineers (backend, frontend and full-stack, data engineering, ML and AI engineering, DevOps and platform, QA and test, architects and tech leads, students and career switchers), each with one short line on what they will use the model for in this course.

slides.title: Learning outcomes
slides.brief: Six learning outcomes of the course, each starting 'You can' with an action the learner can show, and each tagged with the part of the course that teaches it.

slides.title: Before you start
slides.brief: What a learner needs before starting (basic Python, a terminal, git, an account for the model, an optional second key) next to what they do not need (no maths of machine learning, no graphics card, no earlier AI experience).

slides.title: The syllabus
slides.brief: The eleven parts of the course in order, grouped into three units (ideas, evidence, build), each part with its title and planned minutes, so the learner sees how long each part is and where the four small projects and the final project sit.

slides.title: How to read the numbers in this course
slides.brief: Every number in the course is marked as one of two kinds: the company's own claim from a page you can open, or the presenter's own measurement. One real example answer, 0.99, a probability instead of a sentence.

slides.title: The finish-the-sentence game
slides.brief: An everyday picture: a friend says 'The cat sat on the...' and you say 'mat'. A language model plays the same game with text.

slides.title: Text is cut into tokens, and you pay per token
slides.brief: One sentence cut into small pieces called tokens, with input tokens going in and output tokens coming out, each priced per million.

slides.title: A chat model writes one token, then the next
slides.brief: The model writes token one, reads everything again, writes token two, and so on in a loop, so a longer answer takes more steps in order.

slides.title: Chat models and reasoning models
slides.brief: Compare a chat model that answers directly with a reasoning model that writes hidden thinking tokens first: better on hard problems, but slower and more expensive.

slides.title: A clever clerk, and a cash register that only takes yes or no
slides.brief: A human moment: a shop owner asks a clerk 'is this customer angry, yes or no?' and the clerk answers with a long unsure sentence the cash register cannot read.

slides.title: Four problems when software asks a chat model small questions
slides.brief: Four separate problems side by side: wrong answer shape, slow, costs more than the decision is worth, and no honest signal of doubt.

slides.title: Just ask for JSON? It still has to be parsed
slides.brief: The common belief that asking a chat model for JSON solves everything, shown and then corrected: text still has to be read by code, and a fourth team name or an extra sentence breaks it.

slides.title: Right 95 times in 100, but which 5?
slides.brief: Without a doubt signal a person checks all 100 answers. With an honest doubt signal a person checks only the few flagged ones. The same 100 answers, before and after.

slides.title: The smart if-statement
slides.brief: Normal code branches on simple values like amount > 1000. A smart if-statement branches on common sense, like 'is this email angry?', and the answer goes straight into the code path.

slides.title: TypeSafe AI, the company behind Jev
slides.brief: The real home page of the company that makes the model, as it looks today.

slides.title: Where is all the automation?
slides.brief: A short quote from the founder's launch post: models have been superhuman at chat for years, so where is all the automation?

slides.title: From first blog post to open access in seventeen days
slides.brief: Six dated events in September and October 2026, in order on a line: two blog posts, the SDK release, the launch, the waitlist ending, the weak-spots page review.

slides.title: The Coal Question, 1865
slides.brief: The real page of an 1865 economics book with the sentence that cheaper use of coal leads to more coal used, not less.

slides.title: Cheaper to use, so used more
slides.brief: A loop: engines get more efficient, each job costs less coal, so people find many more jobs for engines, so total coal use goes up. TypeSafe expects the same loop for cheap AI decisions.

slides.title: The two big numbers on the home page
slides.brief: The real home page section that says 193.6 times faster and 444.6 times cheaper.

slides.title: Do the division yourself
slides.brief: Working the arithmetic step by step on the example under the big numbers: 8.566 seconds divided by 0.114 seconds is about 75 times, and 0.013880 dollars divided by 0.000081 dollars is about 171 times.

slides.title: Who wrote the answer key?
slides.brief: How the company's own test works: two large models from OpenAI and Anthropic answer every question, their average becomes the answer key, and every model is scored by how often it agrees with that key.

slides.title: TypeSafe's own test: agreement, cost and time
slides.brief: Nine models from the company's own test, each with an agreement score from 53.6 to 74.1 percent and a cost per case from 0.0004 to 0.1761 dollars, placed so you see accuracy against cost.

slides.title: 'Can't hallucinate' means the shape, not the truth
slides.brief: The claim 'zero hallucinations' shown and corrected with the company's own FAQ: the answer is always one of your options, but it can still be the wrong option.

slides.title: Here is the book the name comes from
slides.brief: A real search result page and the publisher page for the 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow.

slides.title: TypeSafe says where the names come from
slides.brief: The real FAQ answer on the launch post that names the book and the economist the product names come from.

slides.title: Fast thinking and slow thinking
slides.brief: Two ways a person thinks, compared side by side with everyday examples: 2 + 2 and a friend's face come instantly; 17 times 24 and a tax form need slow steps. Then the same split for software: a fixed question answered in one go, against a model that writes its reasoning word by word.

slides.title: The bat and the ball
slides.brief: A short puzzle worked step by step: a bat and a ball cost 1.10 dollars, the bat costs 1 dollar more than the ball. The fast answer 10 cents is crossed out, the slow working gives 5 cents.

slides.title: A blank page or a form with tick boxes
slides.brief: A chat model is like a blank page where anything can be written. Jev is like a printed form where you can only tick the boxes that were printed.

slides.title: One request: state and questions in, typed answers out
slides.brief: How one call works: the program sends the material to judge and a set of typed questions, the model returns one typed answer per question with probabilities, and the program acts on them.

slides.title: All questions at once, not word by word
slides.brief: A chat model answers three questions by writing many tokens one after another. Jev answers the same three questions side by side in one pass. The order of work over time is the point.

slides.title: Three question types, three answer shapes
slides.brief: Three question types next to each other: yes or no gives one probability, choice gives one option from a list, score gives a place on a scale you describe.

slides.title: Confidence is the shape of the probabilities
slides.brief: Real probabilities from one run: when most of the probability sits on one option confidence is high, when it is spread out confidence is low. Shown as measured bars.

slides.title: Does a confident answer mean a right answer?
slides.brief: From our own 300 tickets: answers grouped by how confident the model was, and for each group the share that were really right. Honest confidence means the high groups are right more often.

slides.title: Act, check, or hand to a person
slides.brief: One answer's confidence on a scale from 0 to 1 with two cut-off lines marked: below the low line a person decides, between the lines ask to confirm, above the high line the code acts.

slides.title: Where TypeSafe says Jev fits
slides.brief: Five kinds of use the company lists: automation inside software, real-time decisions, processing very large datasets, checking other AIs, and steering an AI agent.

slides.title: Jev in front of the expensive model
slides.brief: An agent system: a user request reaches a fast check first, which routes it, blocks unsafe ones, and only sends the hard ones to a large language model from OpenAI. Real product logos.

slides.title: What a million tickets cost on Jev
slides.brief: Measured cost of sorting support tickets with Jev, from a real run of 300 tickets: 2.5 cents per thousand tickets, scaled up to about 25 US dollars for one million tickets.

slides.title: How to write a good question for Jev
slides.brief: Practical tips from TypeSafe's own guide for writing questions: describe situations instead of bare levels, keep the options clearly different, put the facts in the material, do arithmetic and dates in your own code, keep the material short and relevant.

slides.title: How I made the race fair
slides.brief: The test procedure in order: warm-up calls first, then the models take turns on each item, the order rotates every round, three rounds, then median and slowest-ten-percent are computed.

slides.title: The three models in the race, and their prices
slides.brief: Three models with their published prices per million tokens: one from TypeSafe, a small fast one and a larger one from OpenAI, with the product logos.

slides.title: Ticket triage: time per call
slides.brief: Measured median and 90th percentile seconds per call for three models on the same 40 tickets, three rounds.

slides.title: 300 tickets, eight calls at a time
slides.brief: Measured wall-clock seconds to sort all 300 support tickets with eight calls running at the same time, for three models: 12.6 seconds, 50.1 seconds and 92.8 seconds.

slides.title: What 1,000 tickets cost
slides.brief: Measured US dollars per 1,000 tickets for three models, from each response's real token counts times the published price: 0.0246, 0.0517 and 1.0679 dollars.

slides.title: Three questions in one call
slides.brief: Measured on 30 support tickets: input tokens and seconds when one call asks team, urgency and mood together, against three separate calls, one per question, for each model.

slides.title: A new option from OpenAI: the Decisions API
slides.brief: Measured on the same 300 support tickets on 9 October 2026: Jev against OpenAI's new Decisions API, which also answers typed questions with probabilities. For each, with the product logo: time for all 300 tickets, median time per call, team answers right, cost per 1,000 tickets, price per million input tokens, and whether it can read photos.

slides.title: What Jev gives you on this job
slides.brief: What I measured on ticket sorting: against two OpenAI chat models Jev was faster per call and cheaper; against OpenAI's Decisions API Jev still cost about half as much, but the Decisions API was faster. Every one answered three questions in one call. One short line: OpenAI was more accurate on this job, so test on your own data and use Jev's confidence number.

slides.title: What you need before you start
slides.brief: A checklist of everything to install and set up: Python 3.10 or newer, VS Code, git, the course repository, a virtual environment, the SDK, a TypeSafe account and key, an OpenAI key for the comparisons.

slides.brief: A real terminal showing the command that prints the Python version and its output.

slides.title: Clone the repository and make a virtual environment
slides.brief: A real terminal showing git clone, cd, creating the virtual environment and installing the requirements, with the real output.

slides.title: The repository open in VS Code
slides.brief: The real code editor with the course repository open and its folders visible.

slides.title: The TypeSafe console
slides.brief: The real home page of the TypeSafe console after signing in.

slides.title: Try a question in the Playground first
slides.brief: The real Playground page with an example yes-or-no question and its answer.

slides.title: Create an API key
slides.brief: The real API keys page and the real create-key window, with every secret value blurred.

slides.title: Where the key lives, and where it must never go
slides.brief: How a secret key travels: it sits in a local file or an environment variable, the program reads it at start, it is sent in a request header, and it is never written in code or pushed to GitHub.

slides.title: Your first call, with curl
slides.brief: A real terminal showing the first call to the API with curl and its real JSON answer.

slides.title: Your first call, with Python
slides.brief: A real terminal running the first Python script and its real output.

slides.title: Every claim, and the script that tests it
slides.brief: A list of the company's claims, each next to the name of the exercise script that checks it and what we found.

slides.title: A tiny question still costs about 300 tokens
slides.brief: Measured input tokens for calls with one, three and eight questions, showing a fixed base amount plus a small amount per question.

slides.title: The same request, five times
slides.brief: Five identical requests gave probabilities between 0.41 and 0.51, so one of them crosses the 0.5 line. Shown as measured points around a threshold line.

slides.title: Testing a weak spot: a trick hidden in the input
slides.brief: A real terminal run where a support message contains an instruction meant to trick the model, and the measured effect on the answer.

slides.title: Four small projects, then one big one
slides.brief: Four small projects each add one skill, and all four skills feed into the final project: triage, a check before an answer ships, picking a tool, and a duplicate check, leading to a knowledge graph.

slides.title: Project 1: one ticket, four questions, one call
slides.brief: A support ticket goes in, four typed answers come out, and plain code routes it: send to a team, mark urgent, or put it in the human queue.

slides.title: Project 2: check the draft before the customer sees it
slides.brief: In order: the customer writes, a chat model drafts a reply, Jev checks the draft against the rules, then either the reply is sent or a person reviews it.

slides.title: Project 3: a stricter line for tools that move money
slides.brief: Confidence lines on a scale for an AI agent: safe tools run above 0.60, the refund tool only above 0.85, and below the line the agent asks the user instead.

slides.title: Project 4: are these two records the same company?
slides.brief: Two company records next to each other, field by field, with the differences marked and the answer: same company, a person should check, or different.

slides.title: The big project: from messy records to a knowledge graph
slides.brief: The pipeline in order: make the data, cheap blocking to find candidate pairs, Jev decides each pair, the policy merges or queues, the graph is built, the result is measured against the truth.

slides.title: How one company looks in three systems
slides.brief: The same company written three ways by three systems: different legal suffixes, capital letters, an old city name, a missing website, a different contact person.

slides.title: 266,085 possible pairs down to 1,010
slides.brief: A funnel that narrows: all possible pairs of 730 records, then the pairs that survive cheap blocking, then the duplicates inside them, with every number measured.

slides.title: One score, two cut points, three actions
slides.brief: The pair score from 0 to 2 on a line with cut points at 0.5 and 1.5: below 0.5 keep separate, between a person checks, above 1.5 merge. The measured scores of all 1,014 test pairs shown on the line.

slides.title: The graph before and after
slides.brief: The real graph page in a browser: before, one company appears as three separate nodes with its people split; after, one node holds all its people.

slides.title: Tune the question on the training set
slides.brief: On the training set, the first wording of the middle level sent 159 pairs to a person. Reading them showed the words were taken literally. A clearer wording that says what is normal for a duplicate sent 28. Before and after, measured on the training set.

slides.title: The test set: what Jev decided
slides.brief: Measured on 1,014 test pairs Jev never saw while the wording was tuned: 443 merged and all correct, 543 kept separate and all correct, 28 sent to a person, of which 20 were real duplicates. 41.8 seconds and 3.4 US cents in total.

slides.title: Jev or a chat model?
slides.brief: A simple choice: if the program needs a decision from a fixed list of answers about text, use Jev; if it needs written text for a person, use a chat model. One note: Jev reads text only, so a decision about a photo needs a model that reads images, such as OpenAI's Decisions API.

slides.title: Using both: the cheap check first
slides.brief: A cascade: every request gets a fast, cheap typed check, and only the unclear or hard ones go on to the larger, slower model. Real product logos.

slides.title: Five things to remember
slides.brief: Five practical things to remember about using Jev, on one screen.
